subject: literature
passage: When the new conductor arrived, the orchestra's oldest violinist, Ilse Brandt, had already decided to dislike him. He was too young, she told the others, and he waved his arms as if he were directing traffic. At the first rehearsal she played precisely what was written and nothing more, watching him over the top of her music with an expression she had perfected over thirty years. But midway through the slow movement he stopped the orchestra, turned to her, and asked, quietly, as though it were a real question, how she would phrase the passage. Ilse found, to her irritation, that she had an answer, and that she wanted very much to give it.
stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To show how the conductor's talent quickly wins over every member of the orchestra
choices.B: To depict a moment when a character's fixed hostility begins, against her will, to soften
choices.C: To explain why experienced musicians tend to distrust young conductors
choices.D: To describe the playing techniques Ilse has developed over her long career

explanation.why: Ilse begins having "already decided to dislike" the conductor. The turn comes with "But," when he sincerely asks her opinion, and she finds "to her irritation" that she "wanted very much" to answer. The passage captures her resistance starting to give way even though she does not want it to.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text shows only Ilse's reaction; it says nothing about the rest of the orchestra, and Ilse is not fully won over.
explanation.B: Correct. Ilse's settled dislike starts to weaken when the conductor asks for her view, and "to her irritation" shows this happens against her wishes.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text is about one violinist and one conductor; it does not make a general claim about musicians.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Ilse's practiced expression and exact playing are details used to show her attitude, not the focus of the passage.

checks.note: Best fit on the text alone.
